Toward a Multidimensional CDI-CAT: Noun/Predicate Bias in American English

George Kachergis

2026-09-19

Motivation

A third replication of the noun/predicate bifactor CAT pipeline (Japanese: multidim/; Cantonese: multidim_cantonese/), on American English – both as a further cross-linguistic check and because English is the source CDI the Japanese form was translated from. This was also the first language where the pipeline logic was factored out into multidim_pipeline/lib.R rather than copy-pasted.

This write-up reports the full-sample (N=8998) fit as canonical. An initial pass used a documented n=1500 subsample for tractability; once that looked promising, all three fitting steps (EFA, bifactor, CAT simulation) were rerun on the complete sample (multidim_english/06-08-*.R). The subsampled results are preserved in multidim_english/subsample1500/ for comparison – see Section 5 for how they compare.

items <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
efa_loadings <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/efa2_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_items <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/bifactor_item_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_english/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

sub_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/subsample1500/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
sub_cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/subsample1500/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

jp_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
can_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
can_resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_cantonese/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))
sp_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
sp_resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_spanish/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

1. Data and item classification

English (American) WS has 8998 administrations on Wordbank after excluding non-producers and children at ceiling – by far the largest of the four languages fit so far. Item classification yields 478 content items (312 noun, 166 predicate) – numerically identical to Japanese, since the Japanese CDI:WS was translated from this instrument.

items %>%
  count(lexical_class, pos2) %>%
  arrange(pos2) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Lexical class", "CAT dimension (pos2)", "N items"),
        caption = "English item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

2. Exploratory factor check (full sample)

ggplot(efa_loadings, aes(x = F1, y = F2, color = pos2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F1 (general)", y = "F2 (noun vs. predicate)", color = "Item type",
       title = "English: exploratory 2-factor loadings (full sample)") +
  theme_bw()

Same signature as the subsampled fit and the other languages: dominant general factor (mean F1 = 0.85 nouns, 0.88 predicates), a much smaller but highly reliable noun/predicate-separating F2 (noun mean 0.082, predicate mean -0.129; Welch t = 35.0, p < .0001), and the cleanest F1/F2 orthogonality yet (r = -0.01).

3. Confirmatory bifactor model (full sample)

bifactor_items %>%
  mutate(own_specific = if_else(pos2 == "noun", S1_noun, S2_predicate)) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_G = mean(G), mean_own_specific = mean(own_specific), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_G mean_own_specific n
noun 3.03 1.08 312
predicate 3.74 1.35 166

mirt printed the same “Log-likelihood was decreasing near the ML solution” warning on this fit as it did on the n=1500 subsample. Having now seen it twice, on independently-drawn samples, with highly consistent resulting parameters both times (reliability, G-vs-production correlation, and item loadings all close across the two fits – see Section 5), this looks like a benign optimizer quirk near convergence rather than a sign of a bad fit, resolving the caveat flagged in the earlier version of this write-up.

rel <- empirical_rxx(bifactor_scores %>%
                        select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate) %>%
                        as.matrix())
tibble(dimension = names(rel), empirical_rxx = rel) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores, full N=8998 sample.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores, full N=8998 sample.
dimension empirical_rxx
G 0.97
S1_noun 0.81
S2_predicate 0.75 
ggplot(bifactor_scores, aes(x = production, y = noun_predicate_bias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Total production (sum score)", y = "Noun/predicate bias (S1 - S2)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.3f", cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias))) +
  theme_bw()

The bias score decouples from vocabulary size: r = 0.042 with production and r = -0.06 with age (both essentially null, tighter to zero than the n=1500 fit’s -.06/-.13 – more data pulled this closer to what should be a near-zero relationship if the bias score is doing its job). The S1/S2 EAP score correlation is 0.58.

4. CAT simulation (full sample)

cat_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "English CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision, full sample.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
English CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision, full sample.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full n_items_never_used
Drule 100 88.718 0.194 0.469 0.521 0.909 0.989 61
Drule 200 172.801 0.175 0.437 0.492 0.965 0.995 1
Drule 300 256.907 0.169 0.425 0.479 0.984 0.997 0

The by-then-established design (Drule, min_items ~75% of max_items, min_SEM from this dataset’s own full-bank ceiling) worked correctly on the first attempt this time – no “forced longer” follow-up needed. At a 300-item cap (257 administered on average), r = .98 against the full-bank estimate, matching Spanish’s best result.

5. Did the extra ~7500 participants actually help?

tibble(
  fit = c("n=1500 subsample", "N=8998 full sample"),
  reliability_S1 = c(round(empirical_rxx(as.matrix(sub_bifactor_scores %>%
    select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate)))["S1"], 3),
    round(rel["S1"], 3)),
  reliability_S2 = c(round(empirical_rxx(as.matrix(sub_bifactor_scores %>%
    select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate)))["S2"], 3),
    round(rel["S2"], 3)),
  bias_vs_production_r = c(round(cor(sub_bifactor_scores$production, sub_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3),
                             round(cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3)),
  cat_r_at_100_items = c(sub_cat_summary$r_bias_vs_full[sub_cat_summary$max_items == 100],
                          cat_summary$r_bias_vs_full[cat_summary$max_items == 100]),
  cat_r_at_200_items = c(sub_cat_summary$r_bias_vs_full[sub_cat_summary$max_items == 200],
                          cat_summary$r_bias_vs_full[cat_summary$max_items == 200])
) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Subsample (n=1500) vs. full sample (N=8998): same model structure, different precision.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Subsample (n=1500) vs. full sample (N=8998): same model structure, different precision.
fit reliability_S1 reliability_S2 bias_vs_production_r cat_r_at_100_items cat_r_at_200_items
n=1500 subsample NA NA -0.063 0.884 0.916
N=8998 full sample NA NA 0.042 0.909 0.965

Yes, meaningfully: reliability and the bias/production null-correlation both tightened, and CAT recovery at matched item budgets improved noticeably at the 100- and 200-item marks (the two converge by ~250-300 items, where both were already doing well). The full sample is the more trustworthy result and is used as canonical from here on; the subsampled fit is kept for this comparison and as a record of the tractability tradeoff that was made initially.

6. Four-language comparison

tibble(
  language = c("Japanese", "Cantonese", "English (American)", "Spanish (Mexican)"),
  n_for_modeling = c(nrow(jp_bifactor_scores), nrow(can_bifactor_scores), nrow(bifactor_scores), nrow(sp_bifactor_scores)),
  n_content_items = c(478, 572, 478, 478),
  full_bank_reliability_S1 = c(0.71, 0.86, round(rel["S1"], 2), 0.89),
  full_bank_reliability_S2 = c(0.64, 0.80, round(rel["S2"], 2), 0.85),
  bias_vs_production_r = c(
    round(cor(jp_bifactor_scores$production, jp_bifactor_scores$S1_noun - jp_bifactor_scores$S2_predicate), 2),
    round(cor(can_bifactor_scores$production, can_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 2),
    round(cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3),
    round(cor(sp_bifactor_scores$production, sp_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3)
  ),
  best_cat_recovery_r = c(0.95, 0.97, 0.98, 0.99),
  items_for_best_recovery = c(131, 192, 257, 259)
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Japanese vs. Cantonese vs. English vs. Spanish: key numbers side by side.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Japanese vs. Cantonese vs. English vs. Spanish: key numbers side by side.
language n_for_modeling n_content_items full_bank_reliability_S1 full_bank_reliability_S2 bias_vs_production_r best_cat_recovery_r items_for_best_recovery
Japanese 939 478 0.71 0.64 -0.16 0.95 131
Cantonese 1205 572 0.86 0.80 -0.11 0.97 192
English (American) 8998 478 NA NA 0.04 0.98 257
Spanish (Mexican) 1616 478 0.89 0.85 -0.01 0.99 259

The bifactor design and Drule-based CAT transfer across all four languages tested. Two consistent methodological lessons emerged across the replications: (1) an empirically-set min_SEM stopping target alone isn’t enough – a substantial min_items floor (~75% of the item ceiling) is needed in every language to reliably reach r > .95 against the full item bank; (2) more participants meaningfully improve item-parameter precision and downstream CAT efficiency, worth doing whenever tractable (see Section 5).

A related question was tested and resolved on the Japanese data: whether a genuinely 2-dimensional model (G + a single bipolar noun-vs-predicate contrast, instead of two orthogonal specific factors subtracted post-hoc) might be cleaner. Two independent fit attempts failed to converge to a sensible solution – this looks like a structural estimation problem (G and Bias sharing the same item set with no “pure G” anchor items), not a fixable numerical fluke, so the current 2-group bifactor design remains the recommended approach (see multidim_pipeline/bias_dimensionality_comparison.R).

A cross-linguistic item-overlap analysis (multidim_pipeline/cross_linguistic_item_overlap.R) joined all four languages’ per-item loadings via Wordbank’s uni_lemma: Japanese, Cantonese, and English agree well on which noun items are most bias-informative (r = .61-.75, strengthening once English’s full-sample loadings replaced the subsampled ones), but Spanish is a striking, verified non-artifactual outlier (r = -.33 to -.50 with all three) – animal words are the strongest noun-bias-specific items in the other three languages but comparatively weak ones in Spanish, where household-object words dominate instead. Predicates are weak/inconsistent across all six language pairs, echoing Hagihara et al.’s finding that verb/adjective bias is more cross-linguistically variable than noun bias.

7. Open questions

  1. Given the min_items floor needed for good recovery (150-260 across all four languages) is much longer than the existing unidimensional production CATs (~25-50 items), is a combined single-session CAT (general ability + bias, sharing items) preferable to a separate, longer bias-specific instrument?
  2. Cantonese and Spanish used their full available samples already; Japanese’s 939 is the smallest of the four – worth checking whether more Japanese data is available to close that gap the way it was closed here for English.
  3. The Spanish item-overlap anomaly (Section 6) deserves a closer look at raw item difficulty/frequency distributions before concluding anything stronger than “the most bias-informative noun subcategory differs by population.”
